results.title: Put a Rose Cutting in This Water — 999 Roots By Morning... The Secret AMISH Way
results.description:
There's a rose in a vase on somebody's table right now that's about to be thrown out — and inside that stem is a whole rose bush that nobody will ever grow. Here's why most folks fail at rooting one: a rose cutting almost never dies of hunger. It dies of rot. It sits in water, some fungus gets into that fresh-cut end, and the whole thing turns to mush before a single root forms. Beat the rot and the cutting roots almost by itself — and the two things that beat it are sitting in your kitchen: a clove of garlic and an orange peel. In this video, Amish farmer Jacob Miller shows you how to root a rose cutting in water, for free.

From choosing and stripping the cutting, to the garlic rub that seals the cut wound against infection, to steeping garlic and orange peel into a natural rooting solution, to the damp sponge and plastic-bag greenhouse that keep it from drying out before its roots arrive — this costs nothing at all and needs no bought rooting hormone. Do it right and the cutting begins throwing real roots in about five days. Then pot it on, and you've a rose bush of your own from a single stem that most folks would have binned.

One rose you love can become a whole hedge — and cuttings to give away besides.

🌹 WHAT YOU'LL LEARN

Why cuttings die of ROT, not hunger — and how to beat the only enemy that matters
How to choose and strip a cutting so it puts its strength into roots
The #1 step — rubbing the cut end with garlic to seal it against infection
How to brew a free rooting solution from garlic and orange peel
The damp sponge setup that holds the cutting steady and keeps it from drying out
The plastic-bag greenhouse — and why a rootless cutting can't replace lost water
Where to keep it, when the roots come, and how to pot it on without snapping them
